ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Eight hundred participants were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk and received $0.50 USD upon completion of a 4-minute questionnaire.
Participants were required to be residents of the United States, possess a Mechanical Turk submission approval rating of at least 95%, and pass a CAPTCHA-based verification item.
Participants were presented with two vignettes, each of which described a scenario in which an actor had the choice of sacrificing a single individual to save the lives of five others.
Participants were randomly assigned to either a Deontological or Utilitarian condition.
A sample of 810 U.S. residents was recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiment 1.
Consistent with preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded participants who self-reported engaging in inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to two comprehension check questions.
A sample of 1204 U.S residents was recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiments 1 and 2.
Consistent with preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded participants who self-reported inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to comprehension check items.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three Relationship conditions, which determined the relationship between the known individual and the hypothetical actor in each vignette.
Six hundred and three U.S. residents were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiments 1-3.

Participants were presented with a vignette describing a situation in which two individuals were seeking financial assistance online to help repair flood damage to their homes following a severe storm.
Participants were asked which individual they would donate to if they were in Michael's position: the known individual or the stranger.

Next, participants were informed that the stranger's home had been damaged more severely and would require significantly more money to repair (i.e., compared to the home of Michael's friend, relative, or community member).
Participants randomly assigned to the Public condition were instructed to imagine that their donation decision would be publicly visible online.

Participants were more likely to donate to the known individual rather than the stranger in greater need when the known individual was a friend, OR = 2.62, 95% CI [1.38, 4.96], z = 3.53, p = .001, or relative, OR = 1.95, 95% CI [1.04, 3.63], z = 2.50, p = .033, compared with a community member.
Participants were more likely to donate to the stranger in greater need when their donation decision was private rather than publicly observable, OR = 2.09, 95% CI [1.34, 3.25], z = 3.28, p = .001.

Moreover, this preference was sensitive to social observability: participants were more willing to behave impartially when their decisions were anonymous, consistent with the possibility that publicly observable helping decisions are shaped, in part, by the anticipated social costs of impartiality.
Notably, participants were more likely to choose the impartial option when their decision was described as anonymous rather than publicly observable.
First, the present findings were observed in a sample of U.S. residents recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk, raising questions about the generalizability of these effects across populations.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Eight hundred participants were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk and received $0.50 USD upon completion of a 4-minute questionnaire. Participants were required to be residents of the United States, possess a Mechanical Turk submission approval rating of at least 95%, and pass a CAPTCHA-based verification item. We excluded participants who reported responding randomly at some point during the experiment or failed to correctly respond to two comprehension check items. These exclusion criteria helped promote data quality by removing automated and inattentive responders. The final sample was comprised of 564 participants (47% female; Mage = 39.27, SDage = 12.73). Sensitivity power analyses conducted using G*Power 26 indicated that the retained sample afforded 80% power to detect effects of approximately ηp² = .014 or larger in mixed-model analyses.

A sample of 810 U.S. residents was recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiment 1. Participants received $0.50 USD for completing a 4minute questionnaire. Consistent with preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded participants who self-reported engaging in inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to two comprehension check questions. Our final sample comprised of 497 participants (42% female; Mage = 40.73, SDage = 13.36). Sensitivity power analyses indicated that this sample provided 80% power to detect effects of d = 0.12 or larger in the preregistered paired-samples t-tests.

A sample of 1204 U.S residents was recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiments 1 and 2. Participants received $0.50 USD after completing a 4-minute questionnaire. Consistent with preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded participants who self-reported inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to comprehension check items. Following exclusions, we retained a sample of 901 participants (52% female; Mage = 39.25, SDage = 13.66). Sensitivity power analyses indicated that this sample provided 80% power to detect effects of approximately ηp² = .011 or larger for the preregistered mixed-model analyses.

Six hundred and three U.S. residents were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiments 1-3. Participants received $0.50 USD upon completing a 4-minute questionnaire. We excluded data from 212 participants who self-reported inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to comprehension check questions. The final sample consisted of 391 participants (53% female; Mage = 39.55, SDage = 13.45). Sensitivity power analyses indicated that this sample afforded 80% power to detect effects of ηp² = .024 or larger for the assessed between-subjects interaction.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Predictability and Morality - Social Defection
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
Does socially defecting (e.g., failing to help a close friend) make agents appear immoral and untrustworthy?

Is this due to social defectors being less predictable?

1) Agents who socially defect will be judged as less moral and less trustworthy.
2) Agents who socially defect will be judged as less predictable.
3) Judgments of predictability will be positively associated with trustworthiness and morality.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Participants will judge a hypothetical person on each of the dimensions listed below:

Goodness: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Bad" to "Good"
Morality: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Immoral" to "Moral"
Predictability: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Unpredictable" to "Predictable"
Loyalty: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Disloyal" to "Loyal"
Helpful: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Did not Help" to "Helped a Great Deal"
Obligations: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Completely Violated Obligations" to "Completely Fulfilled Obligations"
Trustworthiness: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Untrustworthy" to "Trustworthy"
Harm: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Caused No Harm" to "Caused a Great Deal of Harm"

Two of our measured variables (i.e., Goodness and Morality) will be averaged to create a moral perception index, previous results have indicated that these variables correlate with alpha = .84 (and above), justifying the index.
table.study_design_overview: All participants will be presented with two moral scenarios (i.e., one featuring an agent socially defecting and one featuring an agent not socially defecting). The order in which these moral scenarios are presented will be counterbalanced.
table.statistical_tests:
Paired samples t-tests will be conducted comparing judgments of moral agents who socially defected versus those who did not socially defect.

Pearson's Correlations will be used to assess the degree of correlation between variables of interest.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participants who fail a comprehension check item will be excluded from analyses.

Participants will also be removed if they answer 'yes' to a data check item asking if there is any reason researchers should not use their data (e.g., due to random responding).
table.sample_size: We will collect a sample of 800 participants on Mechanical Turk.

table.title: Predictability and Morality - Social Defection
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
Does socially defecting (e.g., failing to help a close friend) make agents appear immoral and untrustworthy?

Is this due to social defectors being perceived as less predictable and/or as violating social obligations?

1) Agents who socially defect (i.e., help a stranger instead of a friend or relative) will be judged as less moral and less trustworthy than those who help a close friend or relative (instead of a stranger).
2) Agents who socially defect will be judged as less predictable and as violating obligations to a greater degree.
3) Judgments of predictability will be positively associated with trustworthiness and morality.
4) Judgments of obligations will be positively associated with trustworthiness and morality.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Participants will judge a hypothetical person on each of the dimensions listed below:

Goodness: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Bad" to "Good"
Morality: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Immoral" to "Moral"
Predictability: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Unpredictable" to "Predictable"
Helpful: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Did not Help" to "Helped a Great Deal"
Obligations: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Completely Violated Obligations" to "Completely Fulfilled Obligations"
Trustworthiness: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Untrustworthy" to "Trustworthy"
Harm: Participants will rate a hypothetical person on a 7-point scale that ranges from "Caused No Harm" to "Caused a Great Deal of Harm"

Two of our measured variables (i.e., Goodness and Morality) will be averaged to create a moral perception index.
table.study_design_overview:
Participants will be randomly assigned to one of three between-subjects conditions (Family, Friend, Community Member) for which they will be presented scenarios in which agents will be described as helping/failing to help either relatives, friends, or community members respectively (along with strangers).

All participants will be presented with three moral scenarios (i.e., a social defection item, a non-social defection item, and a no help item). The order in which these moral scenarios are presented will be counterbalanced.
table.statistical_tests:
Mixed ANOVAs will be conducted to examine main effects (e.g., the main effect of item type [social defection, no social defection, no help] on moral perception judgments) and interactions (e.g., the interaction of item type with relation type [family, friend, community member] for moral perception judgments).

T-tests will be conducted to follow-up on main effects and interactions.

Pearson's Correlations will be used to assess the degree of correlation between variables of interest.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participants who fail a comprehension check item will be excluded from analyses.

Participants will also be removed if they answer 'yes' to a data check item asking if there is any reason researchers should not use their data (e.g., due to random responding).

Lastly, we will remove data from those highlighted by Qualtrics BOT detecting software or those who fail our BOT detection item.
table.sample_size: We will collect a sample of 1200 participants on Mechanical Turk.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Your participation is extremely valuable. Purpose In this study you were asked to read a scenario describing moral actions and were asked to make a judgment about individuals committing these actions. We are interested in studying how the predictability of actors influences their perceived morality. The main question we are interested in investigating is, are predictable moral actors perceived as more moral compared to unpredictable moral actors, even when a predictable moral actor causes more harm? To examine this question we showed you scenarios describing an act along with varying additional information about the act. This additional information was given in order to vary the perceived predictability of the moral actors in each scenario. It is hypothesized that participants will perceive predictable moral actors as more “moral” (e.g., “good” as opposed to “bad”) compared to unpredictable actors. Furthermore, we predict that this preference for predictable moral actors will remain even in situations where predictable moral actors cause objectively more harm compared to unpredictable moral actors. Your participation is extremely valuable. Purpose In this study you were asked to read a scenario describing moral actions and were asked to make a judgment about individuals committing these actions. We are interested in studying how the predictability of actors influences their perceived morality. The main question we are interested in investigating is, are predictable moral actors perceived as more moral compared to unpredictable moral actors, even when a predictable moral actor causes more harm? To examine this question we showed you scenarios describing an act along with varying additional information about the act. This additional information was given in order to vary the perceived predictability of the moral actors in each scenario. It is hypothesized that participants will perceive predictable moral actors as more “moral” (e.g., “good” as opposed to “bad”) compared to unpredictable actors. Furthermore, we predict that this preference for predictable moral actors will remain even in situations where predictable moral actors cause objectively more harm compared to unpredictable moral actors. Additional Information When information is transmitted over the internet, privacy cannot be guaranteed. There is always a risk your responses may have been intercepted by a third party (e.g., government agencies, hackers). Qualtrics temporarily collected your MTurk ID and computer IP address to avoid duplicate responses in the dataset but we did not collect information that could identify you personally. The data, with no personal identifiers, collected from this study will be maintained on secure servers at the University of Waterloo. As well, the data will be electronically archived after completion of the study for at least 7 years after which the raw data file may be erased. De-identified data may be submitted to a journal or deposited in online public repositories to support our federal granting agency’s policy on open data and will be presented in aggregate form only in publications. If after receiving this letter, you have any questions about this study or would like additional information to assist you in reaching a decision about participation, please feel free to ask the faculty supervisor listed at the top of this sheet. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 432 columns across 7 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 7 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Eight hundred participants were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk and received $0.50 USD upon completion of a 4-minute questionnaire.
Participants were required to be residents of the United States, possess a Mechanical Turk submission approval rating of at least 95%, and pass a CAPTCHA-based verification item.
Participants were presented with two vignettes, each of which described a scenario in which an actor had the choice of sacrificing a single individual to save the lives of five others.
Participants were randomly assigned to either a Deontological or Utilitarian condition.
A sample of 810 U.S. residents was recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiment 1.
Consistent with preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded participants who self-reported engaging in inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to two comprehension check questions.
A sample of 1204 U.S residents was recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiments 1 and 2.
Consistent with preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded participants who self-reported inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to comprehension check items.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three Relationship conditions, which determined the relationship between the known individual and the hypothetical actor in each vignette.
Six hundred and three U.S. residents were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiments 1-3.

Participants were presented with a vignette describing a situation in which two individuals were seeking financial assistance online to help repair flood damage to their homes following a severe storm.
Participants were asked which individual they would donate to if they were in Michael's position: the known individual or the stranger.

Next, participants were informed that the stranger's home had been damaged more severely and would require significantly more money to repair (i.e., compared to the home of Michael's friend, relative, or community member).
Participants randomly assigned to the Public condition were instructed to imagine that their donation decision would be publicly visible online.

Participants were more likely to donate to the known individual rather than the stranger in greater need when the known individual was a friend, OR = 2.62, 95% CI [1.38, 4.96], z = 3.53, p = .001, or relative, OR = 1.95, 95% CI [1.04, 3.63], z = 2.50, p = .033, compared with a community member.
Participants were more likely to donate to the stranger in greater need when their donation decision was private rather than publicly observable, OR = 2.09, 95% CI [1.34, 3.25], z = 3.28, p = .001.

Moreover, this preference was sensitive to social observability: participants were more willing to behave impartially when their decisions were anonymous, consistent with the possibility that publicly observable helping decisions are shaped, in part, by the anticipated social costs of impartiality.
Notably, participants were more likely to choose the impartial option when their decision was described as anonymous rather than publicly observable.
First, the present findings were observed in a sample of U.S. residents recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk, raising questions about the generalizability of these effects across populations.

#### File paths

**7 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `Morality of Partiality - Exp. #1 - Wide Data.csv` to `../../Data/Experiment 1/Morality of Partiality - Exp. #1 - Wide Data.csv` (in Morality of Partiality - E1 Analyses.R); `Morality of Partiality - Exp. #1 - Long Data.csv` to `../../Data/Experiment 1/Morality of Partiality - Exp. #1 - Long Data.csv` (in Morality of Partiality - E1 Analyses.R); `Morality of Partiality - Exp. #2 - Wide Data.csv` to `../../Data/Experiment 2/Morality of Partiality - Exp. #2 - Wide Data.csv` (in Morality of Partiality - E2 Analyses.R); `Morality of Partiality - Exp. #2 - Long Data.csv` to `../../Data/Experiment 2/Morality of Partiality - Exp. #2 - Long Data.csv` (in Morality of Partiality - E2 Analyses.R); `Morality of Partiality - Exp. #3 - Wide Data.csv` to `../../Data/Experiment 3/Morality of Partiality - Exp. #3 - Wide Data.csv` (in Morality of Partiality - E3 Analyses.R); `Morality of Partiality - Exp. #3 - Long Data.csv` to `../../Data/Experiment 3/Morality of Partiality - Exp. #3 - Long Data.csv` (in Morality of Partiality - E3 Analyses.R); `Morality of Partiality - Exp. #4 - Data.csv` to `../../Data/Experiment 4/Morality of Partiality - Exp. #4 - Data.csv` (in Morality of Partiality - E4 Analyses.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 3 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: While impartiality is often regarded as a moral virtue, acting impartially can violate social expectations and relational obligations, creating tension between competing moral considerations.

The present research (N = 3,417) examined how people evaluate partial and impartial actors who prioritized either a socially connected other (family member, friend, or community member) or a stranger in need.
Across sacrificial dilemmas and more ecologically valid helping scenarios, partial actors were judged more moral and trustworthy than impartial actors.
This preference was strongest when impartial actors failed to prioritize a close (family member or friend), rather than more distant (community member), social tie.
Impartial actors were also perceived as less predictable and as fulfilling less of their relational obligations, with these perceptions predicting judgments of their moral character.
In Experiment 4, participants themselves exhibited a preference for partiality, with most preferring to help a socially connected other over a stranger in greater need.
This preference was stronger when decisions were described as publicly observable rather than anonymous, consistent with reputational concerns influencing helping decisions.

Together, these findings suggest that everyday moral judgments reflect not only assessments of adherence to abstract ethical principles but also inferences about individuals' reliability as long-term social partners.
Whether morality demands impartiality is a longstanding debate in moral philosophy.
Impartial beneficence-the view that everyone's well-being deserves equal moral consideration regardless of one's relationship to them-is regarded as a moral ideal in some ethical traditions 1, 2 .
text.formatted: Impartial beneficence-the view that everyone's well-being deserves equal moral consideration regardless of one's relationship to them-is regarded as a moral ideal in some ethical traditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Yet other theorists argue that prioritizing the well-being of friends and family is a fundamental feature of social relationships 3, 4 .
text.formatted: Yet other theorists argue that prioritizing the well-being of friends and family is a fundamental feature of social relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: This tension raises a central question: how do people judge impartial individuals who neglect to privilege their social ties?
Impartial actions may often convey conflicting moral signals, reflecting moral virtues such as fairness 5 and empathic concern 6 , while simultaneously violating relational expectations 7 .
text.formatted: Impartial actions may often convey conflicting moral signals, reflecting moral virtues such as fairness <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> and empathic concern <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> , while simultaneously violating relational expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: The present research examines how people evaluate the moral character of impartial and partial actors across relational contexts.

We propose that, despite the appeal of impartiality, people exhibit a moral preference for partiality such that they view individuals who prioritize the wellbeing of socially close others as morally superior to those who behave impartially.

Person-centered theories of moral judgment place character assessment at the heart of moral evaluation 8, 9 , viewing moral judgments as less about actions and more about what these actions reveal about a person's underlying character.
text.formatted: Person-centered theories of moral judgment place character assessment at the heart of moral evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> , viewing moral judgments as less about actions and more about what these actions reveal about a person's underlying character.

text.text: People use others' choices not only to infer what kind of person they are, but also how they are likely to behave in the future 10 .
text.formatted: People use others' choices not only to infer what kind of person they are, but also how they are likely to behave in the future <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: From this perspective, impartial helping (e.g., helping a stranger instead of a close other) may support two inferences about the helper, each with distinct implications for moral evaluation.
On the one hand, helping a stranger provides strong evidence of a good moral character as it is less readily explained by situational pressures or self-interest 11 .
text.formatted: On the one hand, helping a stranger provides strong evidence of a good moral character as it is less readily explained by situational pressures or self-interest <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: Consistent with this view, prosocial actions are judged less favorably when they appear to benefit the helper 10, 12 .
text.formatted: Consistent with this view, prosocial actions are judged less favorably when they appear to benefit the helper <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: On the other hand, impartial helping may violate social expectations and signal a lack of loyalty.

Relationship-based theories of morality propose that moral evaluations reflect a psychological adaptation that evolved to facilitate cooperation and maintain social relationships 7, 13, 14 , such that failing to prioritize close others should be seen as a moral violation.
text.formatted: Relationship-based theories of morality propose that moral evaluations reflect a psychological adaptation that evolved to facilitate cooperation and maintain social relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> , such that failing to prioritize close others should be seen as a moral violation.

text.text: Recent research suggests that individuals possess a moral preference for partiality.
People perceive impartial actors electing to help strangers as less moral than partial actors prioritizing the well-being of close others (e.g., family members) [15] [16] [17] [18] .
text.formatted: People perceive impartial actors electing to help strangers as less moral than partial actors prioritizing the well-being of close others (e.g., family members) <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> .

text.text: Relatedly, impartial actors are trusted less and judged as worse cooperation partners, although these judgments do not reliably translate into reduced cooperation during economic games 18, 19 .
text.formatted: Relatedly, impartial actors are trusted less and judged as worse cooperation partners, although these judgments do not reliably translate into reduced cooperation during economic games <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: Yet, the inferences underlying this moral preference and its robustness across relational contexts remain less clear.

One reason people may morally prefer partial actors is that they perceive social relationships as carrying special obligations 7, 13 , obligations that are violated by individuals who fail to prioritize close social ties.
text.formatted: One reason people may morally prefer partial actors is that they perceive social relationships as carrying special obligations <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> , obligations that are violated by individuals who fail to prioritize close social ties.

text.text: The strength of these obligations, and the moral condemnation that follows from violating them, may scale with the degree of social closeness between individuals.

For instance, McManus and colleagues 16 show that people perceive a greater obligation to help close (e.g., siblings) compared to more distant (e.g., cousins) relatives and that perceived obligations are associated with moral evaluations.
text.formatted: For instance, McManus and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> show that people perceive a greater obligation to help close (e.g., siblings) compared to more distant (e.g., cousins) relatives and that perceived obligations are associated with moral evaluations.

text.text: Thus, impartial actors may be viewed as less moral to the extent that their actions violate relational obligations, with the strength of these obligations, and consequently the seriousness of their violation, scaling with social closeness.
Accurately assessing others' character is important for social well-being, allowing people to anticipate others' future behavior and avoid untrustworthy individuals who may cause them harm.
Recent research suggests that people hold a moral preference for more predictable actors, with perceptions of predictability being positively associated with judgments of moral character 20, 21 .
text.formatted: Recent research suggests that people hold a moral preference for more predictable actors, with perceptions of predictability being positively associated with judgments of moral character <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: Thus, in contexts where people expect individuals to prioritize close others, impartial actors may be viewed as less moral because their actions signal unpredictability, with their failure to prioritize close others making their moral beliefs and future behavior difficult to discern.

Furthermore, negative evaluations of impartial actors may be stronger for closer social ties as neglecting to prioritize especially close others may violate people's expectations to a greater extent, thereby providing a stronger signal of an unreliable moral character.

Even if implicitly, the anticipated reputational consequences of different actions play a role in motivating behavior, as suggested by research showing that people more frequently behave in ways that signal their moral quality when others are watching 22, 23 .
text.formatted: Even if implicitly, the anticipated reputational consequences of different actions play a role in motivating behavior, as suggested by research showing that people more frequently behave in ways that signal their moral quality when others are watching <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: As such, the inferences described above may not only shape how people judge partial and impartial actors but also the extent to which they prioritize the well-being of close social ties.
Prior research demonstrates that people direct more help, resources, and altruistic effort toward socially close others than strangers 24, 25 .
text.formatted: Prior research demonstrates that people direct more help, resources, and altruistic effort toward socially close others than strangers <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: If people internalize negative evaluations of impartial actors, they should elect to behave in a more partial manner when their behavior is observable to others.
By doing so, they may not only avoid damaging their social relationships but also be judged more favorably by third-party observers.
The present research investigates how people evaluate the moral character of partial and impartial actors across distinct moral and relational contexts.
Consistent with prior work [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] , we hypothesize that actors prioritizing a socially close other over a stranger will be judged as more moral and trustworthy.
text.formatted: Consistent with prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> , we hypothesize that actors prioritizing a socially close other over a stranger will be judged as more moral and trustworthy.

text.text: We test this hypothesis using both classic sacrificial dilemmas (Experiment 1) and more ecologically valid helping scenarios (Experiments 2 and 3) as well as across relational contexts varying in genetic relatedness (i.e., kin vs. non-kin) and social closeness (e.g., friend vs. community member).
Notably, we also examine when and why impartial actors are judged negatively.
We propose that impartiality is evaluated unfavorably to the extent that it violates relational obligations and social expectations.

Accordingly, Experiments 1-3 test whether impartial actors are perceived as less predictable than partial actors and the extent to which these perceptions of predictability are associated with moral evaluations.
Similarly, Experiments 2 and 3 examine the extent to which impartial actors are viewed as violating relational obligations and whether these perceived violations predict judgments of moral character.

As such, we predict that participants will exhibit a stronger preference for partiality for closer social ties on account that failing to prioritize a close other should be perceived as a greater violation of relational obligations and a stronger signal of unpredictability.
Finally, Experiment 4 examines whether a moral preference for partiality leads people to behave in a more partial manner when their actions are observable to others.
Participants reported whether they would prefer to help a socially connected other (i.e., a friend, family member, or community member) in need or a stranger in greater need.
We hypothesize that participants will generally prefer helping a socially connected other and that this preference will increase with social closeness.

Critically, we predict that participants will behave more partially when their decision is observable to others, consistent with the possibility that people anticipate and seek to avoid negative moral evaluations associated with impartiality.
Eight hundred participants were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk and received $0.50 USD upon completion of a 4-minute questionnaire.
Participants were required to be residents of the United States, possess a Mechanical Turk submission approval rating of at least 95%, and pass a CAPTCHA-based verification item.
We excluded participants who reported responding randomly at some point during the experiment or failed to correctly respond to two comprehension check items.
These exclusion criteria helped promote data quality by removing automated and inattentive responders.
The final sample was comprised of 564 participants (47% female; Mage = 39.27, SDage = 12.73).
Sensitivity power analyses conducted using G*Power 26 indicated that the retained sample afforded 80% power to detect effects of approximately ηp² = .014 or larger in mixed-model analyses.
text.formatted: Sensitivity power analyses conducted using G*Power <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> indicated that the retained sample afforded 80% power to detect effects of approximately ηp² = .014 or larger in mixed-model analyses.

text.text: Participants were presented with two vignettes, each of which described a scenario in which an actor had the choice of sacrificing a single individual to save the lives of five others.
Both vignettes featured a friend of this actor, either as the single individual who could be sacrificed or among the five individuals who could be saved.
Below each vignette was a statement describing whether the actor decided to sacrifice the single individual (Utilitarian Action) or let harm befall five individuals (Deontological Action).
Consequently, this description also revealed whether the actor elected to save their friend (Partial Action) or one or more strangers (Impartial Action).
Following each vignette, participants evaluated the actor across various moral dimensions presented in a randomized order within a matrix table. i Moral Perception.
Participants evaluated each actor's morality and overall goodness using 7-point scales that ranged from immoral to moral and bad to good, respectively.

The two judgments were strongly correlated (Partial Action: r = .87; Impartial Action: r = .89) and were i For the purposes of brevity, secondary measures (empathy, violence, intentionality, and harm) are described and analyzed in the supplementary materials (Parts A and C). averaged to create a moral perception composite, with higher values reflecting stronger perceptions of moral goodness.
Trustworthiness.
Participants judged the trustworthiness of each actor using a 7-point scale that ranged from untrustworthy to trustworthy.
Predictability.
Participants judged the predictability of each actor using a 7-point scale that ranged from unpredictable to predictable.
Participants were randomly assigned to either a Deontological or Utilitarian condition.
In the Deontological condition, participants read two vignettes describing a hypothetical actor who chose not to sacrifice one individual to save five others.

One vignette described the single individual as a friend of the actor (Partial Action), whereas the other described the single individual as a stranger and included the actor's friend among the five individuals who could be saved (Impartial Action).
In contrast, participants in the Utilitarian condition were described a hypothetical actor who chose to sacrifice a single individual to save five others.

Again, one vignette described the single individual as a friend of the actor (Impartial Action) while another described this individual as a stranger and placed the actor's friend among the five people who could be saved (Partial Action).
Accordingly, Experiment 1 featured a 2 (Act Type: Deontological vs.
Utilitarian; between-subjects) by 2 (Partiality: Partial vs.
Impartial Action; within-subjects) mixed design.
The presentation order of partial and impartial vignettes was counterbalanced across participants.
After each vignette, participants evaluated the described actor across various moral dimensions.
Next, they responded to a comprehension check question assessing their understanding of the vignette.
Finally, they concluded Experiment 1 by responding to two demographic questions and a single-item measure of attentiveness.
For all experiments, we collected our full sample prior to data analyses and report all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures used.
All measures and materials presented in the current study can be viewed in the supplementary materials (Part A).
Data, analyses scripts and Qualtrics survey files pertaining to each experiment are available on Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/dhybf/overview?view_only=7266bb4f6d344e619bbdd57a8bf1e294).

text.text: We describe minor deviations from these pre-registrations in the supplementary materials (Part B).
Experiments 1 and 4 were conducted without pre-registration.
First, we examined whether participants exhibited a moral preference for partiality by evaluating actors who chose to save a close friend more favorably than those who behaved impartially.
A 2 (Act Type: Deontological vs.
Utilitarian) by 2 (Partiality: Partial vs.

Impartial Action) mixed ANOVA on moral perceptions revealed a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 562) = 8.36, p = .004, ηp² = .015, such that partial actors were viewed as more moral (M = 4.32, SD = 1.70) than impartial actors (M = 4.20, SD = 1.78).
This effect did not differ across act types, as indicated by the absence of a Partiality by Act Type interaction (p = .823).
Nevertheless, we did observe a main effect of Act Type, F(1, 562) = 221.68, p < .001, ηp² = .283.
text.formatted: Nevertheless, we did observe a main effect of Act Type, F(1, 562) = 221.68, p < .001, ηp² = .283.

text.text: Consistent with prior work 20, 27 , deontological actors were judged as more moral (M = 5.24, SD = 1.28) than utilitarian actors (M = 3.46, SD = 1.51).
text.formatted: Consistent with prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> , deontological actors were judged as more moral (M = 5.24, SD = 1.28) than utilitarian actors (M = 3.46, SD = 1.51).

text.text: The same pattern emerged for judgments of trustworthiness.

Participants evaluated partial actors as more trustworthy than impartial actors, F(1, 562) = 77.54, p < .001, ηp² = .121, and deontological actors as more trustworthy than utilitarian actors, F(1, 562) = 314.75, p < .001, ηp² = .359.
text.formatted: Participants evaluated partial actors as more trustworthy than impartial actors, F(1, 562) = 77.54, p < .001, ηp² = .121, and deontological actors as more trustworthy than utilitarian actors, F(1, 562) = 314.75, p < .001, ηp² = .359.

text.text: Again, the Partiality by Act Type interaction was not significant (p = .126).

Therefore, actors who prioritized the well-being of a close friend were viewed more positively than those behaving impartially, regardless of whether they acted in a deontological or utilitarian manner.
Prior work reveals that more predictable individuals are viewed as more moral and as more desirable cooperation partners, even when their behavior involves causing additional harm 20, 21 .
text.formatted: Prior work reveals that more predictable individuals are viewed as more moral and as more desirable cooperation partners, even when their behavior involves causing additional harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: Thus, we examined whether partial actors were perceived as more predictable than impartial actors, and whether predictability judgments were associated with moral judgments.

A 2 x 2 mixed ANOVA on predictability judgments revealed a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 562) = 143.00, p < .001, ηp² = .203, such that partial actors were perceived as more predictable (M = 4.39, SD = 1.70) than impartial actors (M = 3.71, SD = 1.71).
text.formatted: A 2 x 2 mixed ANOVA on predictability judgments revealed a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 562) = 143.00, p < .001, ηp² = .203, such that partial actors were perceived as more predictable (M = 4.39, SD = 1.70) than impartial actors (M = 3.71, SD = 1.71).

text.text: We also observed a main effect of Act Type, F(1, 562) = 177.26, p < .001, ηp² = .240, with deontological actors perceived as more predictable (M = 4.90, SD = 1.23) than utilitarian actors (M = 3.36, SD = 1.47).
text.formatted: We also observed a main effect of Act Type, F(1, 562) = 177.26, p < .001, ηp² = .240, with deontological actors perceived as more predictable (M = 4.90, SD = 1.23) than utilitarian actors (M = 3.36, SD = 1.47).

text.text: The interaction between Partiality and Act Type was not significant (p = .147).
Next, we examined whether predictability judgments were associated with evaluations of morality and trustworthiness using linear mixed-effects models (Table 1).
text.formatted: Next, we examined whether predictability judgments were associated with evaluations of morality and trustworthiness using linear mixed-effects models (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Predictability was decomposed into within-subject and between-subject components to distinguish participants' general tendency to perceive actors as more or less predictable from actor-specific deviations in predictability judgments.
For moral evaluations, both between-subject and within-subject predictability were positively associated with perceptions of morality (Table 1; Figure 1).
text.formatted: For moral evaluations, both between-subject and within-subject predictability were positively associated with perceptions of morality (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Participants who generally viewed actors as more predictable also tended to view them as more moral, and, within participants, actors judged as more predictable were also judged as more moral.
Act Type remained a significant predictor of moral perceptions when predictability was included in the model, whereas Partiality no longer uniquely predicted moral judgments.
A similar pattern emerged for judgments of trustworthiness (Table 1), although Partiality remained a significant predictor after accounting for perceptions of predictability.
text.formatted: A similar pattern emerged for judgments of trustworthiness (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>), although Partiality remained a significant predictor after accounting for perceptions of predictability.

text.text: In both cases, models including predictability fit the data better than models excluding it (Moral Perceptions: χ 2 (5) = 198.34, p < .001; Trustworthiness: χ 2 (5) = 252.02, p < .001).
text.formatted: In both cases, models including predictability fit the data better than models excluding it (Moral Perceptions: χ 2 (5) = 198.34, p < .001; Trustworthiness: χ 2 (5) = 252.02, p < .001).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that perceptions of predictability play an important role in shaping positive evaluations of partial actors.

Although sacrificial dilemmas are useful for examining moral preferences, they depict extreme situations with low ecological validity 28 .
text.formatted: Although sacrificial dilemmas are useful for examining moral preferences, they depict extreme situations with low ecological validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> .

text.text: Accordingly, in Experiment 2, we examined participants' moral evaluations of partial and impartial actors in more everyday helping contexts, in which actors chose whether to help a friend or a stranger.

Consistent with relationship-based theories of moral judgment 7, 13, 14 , we predicted that participants would again exhibit a moral preference for partiality, evaluating actors who chose to help a friend as more moral and trustworthy than those who instead helped a stranger.
text.formatted: Consistent with relationship-based theories of moral judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> , we predicted that participants would again exhibit a moral preference for partiality, evaluating actors who chose to help a friend as more moral and trustworthy than those who instead helped a stranger.

text.text: Additionally, we examined whether partial actors would be perceived as more predictable and as better fulfilling their relational obligations, and whether these perceptions might help explain positive evaluations of partial actors.
A sample of 810 U.S. residents was recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiment 1.
Participants received $0.50 USD for completing a 4minute questionnaire.
Consistent with preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded participants who self-reported engaging in inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to two comprehension check questions.
Our final sample comprised of 497 participants (42% female; Mage = 40.73, SDage = 13.36).
Sensitivity power analyses indicated that this sample provided 80% power to detect effects of d = 0.12 or larger in the preregistered paired-samples t-tests.
Experiment 2 featured two vignettes adapted from McManus and colleagues 15 .
text.formatted: Experiment 2 featured two vignettes adapted from McManus and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: These vignettes described a situation in which both a hypothetical actor's close friend and a stranger were in need of assistance.
Each vignette was followed by a brief statement describing whether the actor decided to help their friend (Partial Action) or the stranger (Impartial Action).
As in Experiment 1, participants evaluated each actor on several moral dimensions.
Judgments of moral goodness (i.e., moral perceptions), trustworthiness, and predictability were assessed using the same measures as in Experiment 1.
Inspired by relationship-based theories of moral judgment 7, 14 , participants also evaluated the extent to which each actor fulfilled their social obligations.
text.formatted: Inspired by relationship-based theories of moral judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> , participants also evaluated the extent to which each actor fulfilled their social obligations.

text.text: Participants judged the extent to which each actor fulfilled their social obligations using a 7-point scale that ranged from completely violated obligations to completely fulfilled obligations.
Experiment 2 employed a fully within-subjects design.

Participants viewed two vignettes: one in which a hypothetical actor helped a friend rather than a stranger (Partial Action), and one in which an actor helped a stranger rather than a friend (Impartial Action).
The presentation order of vignettes was counterbalanced across participants.
After each vignette, participants evaluated the actor across several moral dimensions and completed a comprehension check item assessing their understanding of the scenario.
Participants then responded to two demographic items and a single-item measure of attentiveness before concluding the experiment.

Consistent with Experiment 1, partial actors were judged as more moral, t(496) = 13.82, p < .001, d = 0.62, 95% CI [0.52, 0.72], and more trustworthy, t(496) = 20.67, p < .001, d = 0.93, 95% CI [0.82, 1.03], than impartial actors.
text.formatted: Consistent with Experiment 1, partial actors were judged as more moral, t(496) = 13.82, p < .001, d = 0.62, 95% CI [0.52, 0.72], and more trustworthy, t(496) = 20.67, p < .001, d = 0.93, 95% CI [0.82, 1.03], than impartial actors.

text.text: Partial actors were also perceived as more predictable, t(496) = 32.23, p < .001, d = 1.45, 95% CI [1.32, 1.57], and as better fulfilling their social obligations, t(496) = 17.10, p < .001, d = 0.77, 95% CI [0.67, 0.87].

text.text: Thus, we again observed a moral preference for partiality, this time within a more ecologically valid helping context.
Actors who prioritized the well-being of a friend were viewed as more moral, trustworthy, and predictable, while also being perceived as better fulfilling their relational obligations.
Next, we examined whether judgments of predictability and social obligation were associated with moral evaluations.
As in Experiment 1, predictability judgments were decomposed into within-subject and between-subject components.
The same decomposition was applied to judgments of social obligation.
Both within-subject and between-subject variation in perceived predictability and social obligation were positively associated with moral perceptions (Table 2).
text.formatted: Both within-subject and between-subject variation in perceived predictability and social obligation were positively associated with moral perceptions (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Participants who generally perceived actors as more predictable and as better fulfilling their social obligations also tended to view them as more moral.
Likewise, within participants, actors perceived as more predictable and as better fulfilling their social obligations were also judged as more moral.
Importantly, Partiality no longer predicted moral evaluations after accounting for predictability and social obligation judgments.

We also observed a Partiality by Predictability interaction (Table 2; Figure 2), such that predictability was positively associated with moral evaluations for partial actors, b = 0.23, 95% CI [0.14, 0.31], t(930) = 5.00, p < .001, but was not reliably associated with evaluations of impartial actors, b = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.16, 0.01], t(930) = -1.65, p = .099.

text.text: Model comparisons indicated that including predictability and social obligation judgments substantially improved model fit relative to models excluding one or both predictors (all χ 2 > 33.53, all p < .001).

Experiments 1 and 2 revealed a moral preference for actors who prioritized close others over strangers.
In Experiment 3, we examined whether this preference varies across different social relationships.
People are generally more willing to help family members than friends, and friends than strangers 24, 29 and perceive stronger obligations toward closer ties 7, 16 .
text.formatted: People are generally more willing to help family members than friends, and friends than strangers <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> and perceive stronger obligations toward closer ties <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> .

text.text: Accordingly, we manipulated whether the known individual in need of assistance was a family member, friend, or community member to examine whether participants' preference for partiality varies across relational contexts, and, importantly, whether perceptions of predictability and social obligation help explain moral evaluations of partial and impartial actors across these contexts.
A sample of 1204 U.S residents was recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiments 1 and 2.
Participants received $0.50 USD after completing a 4-minute questionnaire.
Consistent with preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded participants who self-reported inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to comprehension check items.
Following exclusions, we retained a sample of 901 participants (52% female; Mage = 39.25, SDage = 13.66).
Sensitivity power analyses indicated that this sample provided 80% power to detect effects of approximately ηp² = .011 or larger for the preregistered mixed-model analyses.
Experiment 3 featured three vignettes, two of which were identical to those used in Experiment 2.
Each vignette described a situation in which both a stranger and a known individual required help.
Depending on condition, the known individual was described as a close friend, relative, or member of the same community as a hypothetical actor able to provide help.

Following each vignette, participants read a brief statement indicating whether the actor chose to help the known individual (Partial Action), the stranger (Impartial Action), or neither individual (No Help Action).
Participants then evaluated each actor on the same moral dimensions assessed in Experiment 2.
Experiment 3 featured a 3 (Relationship: Friend, Relative, Community Member; between-subjects) by 3 (Partiality: Partial Action, Impartial Action, No Help Action; withinsubjects) mixed design.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three Relationship conditions, which determined the relationship between the known individual and the hypothetical actor in each vignette.

Regardless of condition, participants viewed three vignettes: one in which the actor helped the known individual, one in which they helped the stranger, and one in which they chose not to help either individual.
The pairing of actions with vignettes, and the presentation order of the resulting items, was counterbalanced, such that each combination and order was equally likely to occur.

Because the present research focuses on moral evaluations of partial versus impartial actions, judgments of actors who chose not to help either individual were not analyzed here, as these actors differed not in whom they helped, but in whether they helped at all. ii Following each vignette, participants judged the actor on various moral dimensions and responded to a comprehension check question.

Participants then completed three items assessing their beliefs about the morality of helping family, friends, and community members before strangers, followed by two demographic questions and a single-item measure of attentiveness.
ii Not surprisingly, actors who chose not to help either individual were judged as less moral and trustworthy than both partial and impartial actors (all p < .001, all d > 0.62).

text.text: We conducted a 3 (Relationship: Friend, Relative, Community Member) by 2 (Partiality: Partial Action, Impartial Action) mixed ANOVA to test whether partial actors were perceived as more moral than impartial actors and whether the magnitude of this effect varied across relationship contexts.
This analysis revealed a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 898) = 330.49, p < .001, ηp² = .269.
text.formatted: This analysis revealed a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 898) = 330.49, p < .001, ηp² = .269.

text.text: As hypothesized, partial actors were judged as more moral (M = 5.65, SD = 1.09) than impartial actors (M = 4.70, SD = 1.38).
We also observed a Partiality by Relationship interaction, F(2, 898) = 10.79, p < .001, ηp² = .023 (Figure 3).

There was a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 898) = 629.45, p < .001, ηp² = .412, as well as a Partiality by Relationship interaction, F(2, 898) = 6.96, p = .001, ηp² = .015.

Thus, these findings suggest that relational closeness amplifies individuals' moral preference for partiality.

iii Moral evaluations of partial and impartial actors were consistent with participants' explicit beliefs about the morality of prioritizing close others over strangers (Supplementary Materials Part C).

Next, we examined whether partial actors were again perceived as more predictable and as better fulfilling their social obligations, and whether the magnitude of these effects varied across relationship contexts.

Analyses of predictability judgments revealed a main effect of Partiality, F(1, 898) = 2233.91, p < .001, ηp² = .713, as well as a significant Partiality by Relationship interaction, F(2, 898) = 10.66, p < .001, ηp² = .023.

text.text: Thus, partial actors were again viewed as more predictable and as fulfilling more of their social obligations than impartial actors, particularly when prioritizing socially close-relative to more distant-social ties.
Finally, we examined whether judgments of predictability and social obligation were associated with moral evaluations using linear mixed-effects models.
As in Experiment 2, predictability and social obligation judgments were decomposed into within-subject and between-subject components.
Replicating the results of Experiment 2, both within-subject and between-subject variation in these judgments were positively associated with perceptions of moral goodness (Table 3).
text.formatted: Replicating the results of Experiment 2, both within-subject and between-subject variation in these judgments were positively associated with perceptions of moral goodness (Table <ref type="table">3</ref>).

text.text: That is, perceiving actors, in general, as more predictable and as fulfilling more of their social obligations was associated with judging them as more moral.
Similarly, within participants, actors viewed as more predictable and as better fulfilling their social obligations were also viewed as more moral.
Notably, Partiality was no longer a reliable predictor of moral evaluations after accounting for predictability and social obligation judgments (Table 3).
