Experiments 1-3 demonstrated that people view individuals who prioritize close others over strangers as more moral and trustworthy.
Experiment 4 examined whether this moral preference is reflected in individuals' own helping decisions.
Participants chose whether to help a socially close other or a stranger in greater need, allowing us to assess whether people themselves prioritize close others in everyday helping contexts.
We also examined whether anonymity moderates these decisions.

If people have internalized social norms favoring partiality, they should be more likely to prioritize close others when their behavior is publicly observable, given that failing to do so may not only risk damaging an important relationship but lead to negative moral evaluations from observers.
Accordingly, we predicted that participants would be more likely to behave partially when their choices were public rather than private.
Six hundred and three U.S. residents were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk using the same eligibility criteria as Experiments 1-3.
Participants received $0.50 USD upon completing a 4-minute questionnaire.
We excluded data from 212 participants who self-reported inattentive responding or failed to correctly respond to comprehension check questions.
The final sample consisted of 391 participants (53% female; Mage = 39.55, SDage = 13.45).
Sensitivity power analyses indicated that this sample afforded 80% power to detect effects of ηp² = .024 or larger for the assessed between-subjects interaction.

Participants were presented with a vignette describing a situation in which two individuals were seeking financial assistance online to help repair flood damage to their homes following a severe storm.
Within the vignette, participants read about a hypothetical actor ("Michael") who had decided to donate $100 to one of these individuals.

One individual was described as socially connected to Michael-either his friend, relative, or a member of his community, depending on Relationship condition-whereas the other individual was described as a stranger.
Participants were asked which individual they would donate to if they were in Michael's position: the known individual or the stranger.
They then responded to the question, "How difficult would this decision be for you?"
using a 7-point scale that ranged from 1 (Not at all difficult) to 7 (Extremely difficult).

Next, participants were informed that the stranger's home had been damaged more severely and would require significantly more money to repair (i.e., compared to the home of Michael's friend, relative, or community member).
Participants again indicated which individual they would donate to and rated how difficult this decision would be using the same 7-point scale.
Thus, the second donation decision assessed whether participants would prioritize a socially close other even when a stranger was in greater need.
Experiment 4 featured a 3 (Relationship: Friend, Relative, Community Member) by 2 (Donation Anonymity: Public, Private) between-subjects design.
Participants randomly assigned to the Public condition were instructed to imagine that their donation decision would be publicly visible online.
Conversely, those assigned to the Private condition were told that their decision would remain completely anonymous.

Following the donation task, participants responded to a comprehension check question and exploratory measures assessing whether they prioritize being helpful or appearing helpful (Supplementary Materials Part A).
They concluded Experiment 4 by responding to two demographic questions and a single-item measure of attentiveness.
Participants exhibited a strong preference for partiality in their donation decisions.
When a known individual and a stranger were described as being in equal need, a large majority of participants (97%) elected to donate to the known individual, χ 2 (1) = 340.73, p < .001.
text.formatted: When a known individual and a stranger were described as being in equal need, a large majority of participants (97%) elected to donate to the known individual, χ 2 (1) = 340.73, p < .001.

text.text: Even after learning that the stranger was in greater need, a smaller-but still clear-majority of participants (66%) continued to prioritize the known individual, χ 2 (1) = 42.56, p < .001 (Figure 5).
text.formatted: Even after learning that the stranger was in greater need, a smaller-but still clear-majority of participants (66%) continued to prioritize the known individual, χ 2 (1) = 42.56, p < .001 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref>).

text.text: We used binary logistic regressions to examine whether Relationship (Friend, Relative, Community Member), Donation Anonymity (Public, Private), and their interaction predicted participants' donation decisions.

We focused on participants' second donation choice-made after learning that the stranger was in greater need-because participants overwhelmingly chose to donate to the known individual prior to this information, regardless of condition.
Analyses of participants' second donation choice revealed a main effect of Relationship, χ 2 (2) = 13.79, p = .001.

Participants were more likely to donate to the known individual rather than the stranger in greater need when the known individual was a friend, OR = 2.62, 95% CI [1.38, 4.96], z = 3.53, p = .001, or relative, OR = 1.95, 95% CI [1.04, 3.63], z = 2.50, p = .033, compared with a community member.
Thus, preferences for partiality were stronger in the case of close, rather than more distant, social ties. v We also observed a main effect of Donation Anonymity, χ 2 (1) = 11.00, p < .001.
text.formatted: Thus, preferences for partiality were stronger in the case of close, rather than more distant, social ties. <ref type="bibr">v</ref> We also observed a main effect of Donation Anonymity, χ 2 (1) = 11.00, p < .001.

text.text: Participants were more likely to donate to the stranger in greater need when their donation decision was private rather than publicly observable, OR = 2.09, 95% CI [1.34, 3.25], z = 3.28, p = .001.

Thus, observability increased participants' tendency to prioritize socially close others, suggesting that participants may have been aware of and considered the reputational consequences of impartiality.
v Participants' donation decisions were again consistent with their explicit beliefs about the morality of prioritizing close others over strangers (Supplementary Materials Part C).
We next examined judgments of decision difficulty using a 3 x 2 between-subjects ANOVA.

This analysis revealed a main effect of Relationship, F(2, 385) = 3.03, p = .049, ηp² = .016, such that participants reported greater difficulty deciding whom to help when the known individual was more socially distant.
In contrast, Donation Anonymity did not influence decision difficulty, F(1, 385) = 0.46, p = .500, ηp² = .001.
Thus, although anonymity altered participants' donation choices, it did not appear to change the subjective difficulty of the moral conflict itself.

We did not observe a Relationship by Donation Anonymity interaction for either donation decisions, χ 2 (2) = 0.23, p = .893, or judgments of decision difficulty, F(2, 385) = 0.27, p = .761, ηp² = .001.
Taken together, these findings suggest that individuals exhibit a robust behavioral preference for partiality, even when a stranger is objectively in greater need of help.

Moreover, this preference was sensitive to social observability: participants were more willing to behave impartially when their decisions were anonymous, consistent with the possibility that publicly observable helping decisions are shaped, in part, by the anticipated social costs of impartiality.
Participants demonstrated a consistent moral preference for partiality.
Actors who prioritized socially close others over strangers were judged as more moral and trustworthy across both classic sacrificial dilemmas and more ecologically valid helping contexts.
Thus, despite impartial beneficence being a central tenet of many moral philosophies 1,2 , everyday moral judgments appear to favor those who prioritize close others.
The present research provides insight into why impartial actors are viewed less favorably.

Across experiments, impartial actors were perceived as less predictable and as fulfilling less of their social obligations, with these perceptions being associated with less favorable moral evaluations.

Thus, moral evaluations of impartial actors may not simply reflect the perceived morality of their actions, but assessments of what these actions reveal about their reliability as long-term cooperation partners.
Moral judgments have been theorized to serve as a psychological adaptation that facilitates cooperation 7, 13, 14 .
text.formatted: Moral judgments have been theorized to serve as a psychological adaptation that facilitates cooperation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: Accordingly, individuals who defy social expectations or violate relational obligations, even when helping strangers, may be viewed as immoral or untrustworthy because their actions signal poor relational reliability.
That is, failing to prioritize close others may signal than an individual is unlikely to honor the obligations associated with close relationships.

Similarly, impartial actions, when defying social expectations, may make a person's motives and future behavior more difficult to discern, generating social uncertainty and undermining trust 20, 21, 30 .
text.formatted: Similarly, impartial actions, when defying social expectations, may make a person's motives and future behavior more difficult to discern, generating social uncertainty and undermining trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> .

text.text: Although the present research cannot establish the precise causal role of these perceptions, the robust associations observed across paradigms suggest that perceived unpredictability and relational violations contribute to the reputational costs of impartiality.
The present findings also highlight the importance of relational context in moral judgment.
Although moral psychology has traditionally ignored the role of social relationships 28 , recent work has begun to examine how relationships shape moral evaluations [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] 31 .
text.formatted: Although moral psychology has traditionally ignored the role of social relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> , recent work has begun to examine how relationships shape moral evaluations <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> .

text.text: Building on this work, the present findings demonstrate that the moral preference for partiality varies across relational contexts.
Actors who failed to prioritize a family member or friend were judged more negatively than those who failed to prioritize a member of their community.

Judgments of predictability and social obligation were similarly influenced by relational context: impartial actors were viewed as less predictable and as violating their social obligations to a greater extent when they failed to help socially close rather than more distant others.
Thus, the reputational costs of impartiality depend, in part, on the closeness of the relationship being neglected.
A preference for partiality also emerged in participants' own helping decisions.
In Experiment 4, most participants preferred to help a socially connected other over a stranger, even when the stranger was in greater need.
This preference was particularly pronounced when the familiar other was a close social tie (e.g., friend).
Notably, participants were more likely to choose the impartial option when their decision was described as anonymous rather than publicly observable.

This finding suggests that helping decision are shaped by reputational concerns, with publicly failing to help a close social tie risking not only relational strain with the neglected individual but moral condemnation from observers.

These findings extend prior research showing that prosocial behavior increases under observation 22, 32, 33 by suggesting that observation shapes not only whether people behave generously, but also whom they choose to help.
text.formatted: These findings extend prior research showing that prosocial behavior increases under observation <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> by suggesting that observation shapes not only whether people behave generously, but also whom they choose to help.

text.text: More broadly, they highlight a potential tension between impartial moral ideals and the relational expectations that shape everyday moral behavior.

People may regard impartiality as morally admirable in principle while nevertheless anticipating negative social consequences for acting impartially in contexts where close others are expected to receive priority.
This tension may be particularly relevant for effective altruism movements, which encourage adherents not only to endorse impartiality as a moral ideal but also to act on it publicly.
The present findings suggest that, at least in some interpersonal contexts, impartial helping carries reputational costs, particularly when it involves neglecting close social ties.
Consequently, promoting impartial giving may require not only appealing to aggregate welfare and fairness, but also addressing the relational expectations that shape everyday moral evaluations.
The present work is not without limitations.
First, the present findings were observed in a sample of U.S. residents recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk, raising questions about the generalizability of these effects across populations.

Although prior work suggests that perceptions of relational obligations and preferences for predictable social partners are widespread 14, 20 cultural variation likely exists in the extent to which partiality is morally valued.
text.formatted: Although prior work suggests that perceptions of relational obligations and preferences for predictable social partners are widespread <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> cultural variation likely exists in the extent to which partiality is morally valued.

text.text: Future research should seek to examine these effects in non-WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) populations, including within cultures that place differing emphasis on collectivism and kinship obligations.
Second, the present research relied on hypothetical vignettes and self-reported donation preferences.
Although such methods are common in moral psychology, they necessarily simplify the complexity of moral decisions in real interpersonal contexts.
Future research could examine whether similar patterns emerge in behavioral paradigms involving real financial stakes or repeated cooperation.

For example, it would be informative to assess whether people preferentially cooperate with impartial actors in interactive economic games, and whether such behavior is mediated by perceptions of predictability or relational obligations.
Similarly, future work may examine whether real-world donation decisions exhibit a preference for partiality and whether this preference is mitigated by anonymity.
Across four experiments, people consistently preferred actors who prioritized close others over strangers.

Partial actors were viewed as more predictable and as better fulfilling their social obligations than impartial actors, and these perceptions were associated with more favorable judgments of their moral character.
Participants' own prosocial preferences also exhibited partiality, with most electing to help a socially connected other even when a stranger was in greater need.
Despite the moral appeal of impartiality 1, 2, 6 , the present findings suggest that everyday moral judgments are deeply shaped by relational obligations and concerns about social reliability.
text.formatted: Despite the moral appeal of impartiality <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> , the present findings suggest that everyday moral judgments are deeply shaped by relational obligations and concerns about social reliability.

text.text: Thus, moral evaluations may be guided less by detached assessments of whether actions conform to abstract moral principles and more by pragmatic inferences about what those actions reveal about a person's value as a long-term cooperation partner.
